claim: Sensory neurons achieve optimal encoding by matching their tuning properties to the natural stimulus statistics.
source: Growing evidence suggests that sensory neurons achieve optimal encoding by matching their tuning properties to the natural stimulus statistics.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to established research in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'growing evidence suggests'.

claim: Feedback pathways from higher brain areas mediate optimized encoding of naturalistic stimuli via temporal whitening in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
source: Here we demonstrate that feedback pathways from higher brain areas mediate optimized encoding of naturalistic stimuli via temporal whitening in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: One source of direct feedback uniformly enhances neural responses.
source: While one source of direct feedback uniformly enhances neural responses, a separate source of indirect feedback selectively attenuates responses to low frequencies, thus creating a high-pass neural tuning curve that opposes the decaying spectral power of natural stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulations and neural recordings presented in the results section.

claim: Indirect feedback selectively attenuates responses to low frequencies, creating a high-pass neural tuning curve that opposes the decaying spectral power of natural stimuli.
source: While one source of direct feedback uniformly enhances neural responses, a separate source of indirect feedback selectively attenuates responses to low frequencies, thus creating a high-pass neural tuning curve that opposes the decaying spectral power of natural stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulations showing differential effects of indirect feedback inactivation.

claim: One population of higher brain neurons displayed broadband tuning.
source: While one population displayed broadband tuning, the other displayed high-pass tuning and thus performed temporal whitening.
evidence: This is supported by recordings from nP stellate cells showing frequency-independent tuning.

claim: One population of higher brain neurons displayed high-pass tuning and performed temporal whitening.
source: While one population displayed broadband tuning, the other displayed high-pass tuning and thus performed temporal whitening.
evidence: This is supported by recordings from nP multipolar cells showing high-pass tuning characteristics.

claim: Efficient coding is achieved by ensuring that the neural tuning function is inversely proportional to stimulus intensity as a function of frequency, thereby achieving a neural response whose amplitude is independent of frequency.
source: Theory posits that efficient coding is achieved by ensuring that the neural tuning function is inversely proportional to stimulus intensity as a function of frequency, thereby achieving a neural response whose amplitude is independent of frequency (Rieke et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work by Rieke et al., 1996.

claim: Whitening has been observed across species and systems.
source: While such 'whitening' has been observed across species and systems (Dan et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2016; Pozzorini et al., 2013; Pitkow and Meister, 2012), the nature of the underlying mechanisms remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies across different systems.

claim: The nature of the mechanisms underlying whitening remains unclear.
source: While such 'whitening' has been observed across species and systems (Dan et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2016; Pozzorini et al., 2013; Pitkow and Meister, 2012), the nature of the underlying mechanisms remains unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Weakly electric fish generate a quasi-sinusoidal signal called the electric organ discharge (EOD) around their body.
source: These fish generate a quasi-sinusoidal signal called the electric organ discharge (EOD) around their body, thereby allowing them to explore the environment and communicate with conspecifics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biology of weakly electric fish.

claim: When two conspecifics are located close (<1 m) to one another, each fish experiences an amplitude modulation of its own EOD.
source: When two conspecifics are located close (<1 m) to one another, each fish experiences an amplitude modulation of its own EOD (i.e., a beat or first-order) whose amplitude (i.e., envelope or second-order) is a function of the distance and relative orientation between two conspecifics (Yu et al., 2012; Fotowat et al., 2013) (see (Stamper et al., 2013) for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Natural electrosensory envelopes due to movement measured in freely moving animals display scale invariance in that their spectral power decays as a power law as a function of increasing temporal frequency.
source: Natural electrosensory envelopes due to movement measured in freely moving animals display scale invariance in that their spectral power decays as a power law as a function of increasing temporal frequency (Fotowat et al., 2013; Metzen and Chacron, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing natural stimuli.

claim: Weakly electric fish give robust behavioral responses to movement related envelopes in which the EOD frequency tracks the stimulus' detailed time course.
source: Weakly electric fish furthermore give robust behavioral responses to movement related envelopes in which the EOD frequency tracks the stimulus' detailed (Metzen and Chacron, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous behavioral study.

claim: Peripheral receptors project to pyramidal cells within the electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL) which in turn project to higher brain structures, thereby giving rise to behavior.
source: These project to pyramidal cells within the electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL) which in turn project to higher brain structures, thereby giving rise to behavior (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the anatomical organization of the electrosensory system, supported by the schematic in Figure 1B.

claim: ELL pyramidal cells receive large amounts of descending inputs (i.e., feedback) from higher brain centers such as the nucleus praeeminentialis (nP).
source: ELL pyramidal cells also receive large amounts of descending inputs (i.e., feedback) from higher brain centers such as the nucleus praeeminentialis (nP) and contact ELL pyramidal cells either directly (i.e., the direct feedback pathway) or indirectly (i.e., the indirect feedback pathway; Figure 1B) (Berman and Maler, 1999; Sas and Maler, 1983; Sas and Maler, 1987).
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Both direct and indirect feedback inputs play important roles in shaping pyramidal cell responses to beats and other first-order electrosensory stimuli.
source: Pyramidal cell responses to beats and other first-order electrosensory stimuli are well characterized in general (see (Clarke et al., 2015; Chacron et al., 2011; Marsat et al., 2012; Krahe and Maler, 2014; Huang and Chacron, 2017) for review) and several studies have shown that both direct and indirect feedback inputs play important roles in shaping (Bastian, 1986a; Bastian et al., 2004; Bastian, 1999; Bol et al., 2011; Chacron, 2006; Chacron et al., 2005) as well as synthesizing (Clarke and Maler, 2017) these.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ELL pyramidal cells can optimally encode natural electrosensory envelopes because their high-pass tuning properties effectively oppose the decaying stimulus power, such that the response power is whitened.
source: Specifically, it was shown that ELL pyramidal cells can optimally encode natural electrosensory envelopes because their high-pass tuning properties effectively oppose the decaying stimulus power, such that the response power is whitened (Huang et al., 2016; Zhang and Chacron, 2016; Huang and Chacron, 2016; Martinez et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies from the same research group.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation strongly reduced pyramidal cell and behavioral responses to envelopes.
source: Pharmacological inactivation of all sources of descending input strongly reduced pyramidal cell and behavioral responses to envelopes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: After complete feedback inactivation, pyramidal cell responses to high envelope frequencies were relatively more attenuated than those to low envelope frequencies.
source: However, pyramidal cell responses to high envelope frequencies were relatively more attenuated than those to low envelope frequencies, such that the resulting tuning was no longer high-pass but independent of envelope frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning curve data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation compromised optimized coding of natural stimuli by temporal whitening.
source: As a consequence, optimized coding of natural stimuli by temporal whitening was compromised.
evidence: This claim is supported by the white index measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Selective inactivation of indirect feedback input strongly increased both pyramidal cell and behavioral sensitivity to envelopes.
source: In contrast, selective inactivation of indirect feedback input strongly increased both pyramidal cell and behavioral sensitivity to envelopes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: After indirect feedback inactivation, enhancement was primarily seen for low envelope frequencies, such that the resulting pyramidal cell tuning curve was broadband.
source: However, enhancement was primarily seen for low envelope frequencies, such that the resulting pyramidal cell tuning curve was broadband, which also compromised optimized coding of natural stimuli by temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning curve data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: nP neurons projecting directly to ELL displayed broadband envelope frequency tuning curves and did not perform temporal whitening.
source: nP neurons projecting directly to ELL displayed broadband envelope frequency tuning curves and thus did not perform temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by recordings from nP stellate cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: nP neurons projecting indirectly to ELL displayed high-pass envelope frequency tuning curves that effectively opposed the decaying envelope stimulus spectral power content, thereby enabling temporal whitening.
source: In contrast, nP neurons projecting indirectly to ELL displayed high-pass envelope frequency tuning curves that effectively opposed the decaying envelope stimulus spectral power content, thereby enabling temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by recordings from nP multipolar cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation did not affect ELL pyramidal cell responses to AMs.
source: Interestingly, complete feedback inactivation did not affect ELL pyramidal cell responses to AMs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered average data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Performing a 'Sham complete feedback inactivation' by injecting saline instead of lidocaine bilaterally into nP did not alter neural or behavioral responses to envelopes.
source: We note that performing a 'Sham complete feedback inactivation' by injecting saline instead of lidocaine bilaterally into nP did not alter neural or behavioral responses to envelopes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This control experiment is documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Injecting lidocaine unilaterally within the contralateral nP while recording from pyramidal cells within the ipsilateral ELL gave rise to similar changes in neural responses to envelopes as bilateral injection.
source: Finally, our results showing that complete feedback inactivation strongly affects ELL neural responses to envelopes were robust. This is because injecting lidocaine unilaterally within the contralateral nP while recording from pyramidal cells within the ipsilateral ELL gave rise to similar changes in neural responses to envelopes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lidocaine injection into PET increased ELL pyramidal neuron responses to AMs.
source: Consistent with previous results, lidocaine injection increased ELL pyramidal neuron responses to AMs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered average data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Inactivating indirect feedback by injecting CNQX in the ELL molecular layer gave rise to similar effects on ELL pyramidal cell responses to envelopes as lidocaine injection into PET.
source: We note that inactivating indirect feedback by injecting CNQX in the ELL molecular layer (Figure 3C) gave rise to similar effects on ELL pyramidal cell responses to envelopes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CNQX injection in the ELL molecular layer significantly increased ELL pyramidal cell responses to AMs.
source: Also, consistent with previous results (Bastian et al., 2004), this manipulation significantly increased ELL pyramidal cell responses to AMs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered average data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: nP stellate cells project directly to ELL pyramidal cells while nP multipolar cells project indirectly through the EGp.
source: Specifically, nP stellate cells project directly to ELL pyramidal cells while nP multipolar cells instead project indirectly through the EGp (Sas and Maler, 1983; Sas and Maler, 1987).
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Both stellate and multipolar cell types can be distinguished from one another based on their electrophysiological properties.
source: Both cell types can easily be distinguished from one another based on their electrophysiological properties (Bastian and Bratton, 1990; Bratton and Bastian, 1990) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both stellate and multipolar cells responded strongly to envelopes.
source: Overall, our results show that both stellate and multipolar cells responded strongly to envelopes (Figure 6B) but showed differential envelope frequency tuning (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by neural response data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Stellate and multipolar cells showed differential envelope frequency tuning.
source: Overall, our results show that both stellate and multipolar cells responded strongly to envelopes (Figure 6B) but showed differential envelope frequency tuning (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by tuning curve data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Stellate cell sensitivity was largely independent of envelope frequency.
source: Specifically, stellate cell sensitivity was largely independent of envelope frequency (Figure 6C, brown) as quantified by a power law exponent near zero (Figure 6E, left panel, brown).
evidence: This claim is supported by tuning curve and exponent data shown in Figure 6C and 6E.

claim: Stellate cells did not perform temporal whitening of natural envelopes as their response power spectra decayed with increasing frequency.
source: As such, these cells did not perform temporal whitening of natural envelopes as their response power spectra decayed with increasing frequency (Figure 6D and E right, brown).
evidence: This claim is supported by response power and white index data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: The function of the direct feedback input is to enhance ELL pyramidal cell responses to envelopes independently of temporal frequency.
source: These results confirm our hypothesis that the function of the direct feedback input is to enhance ELL pyramidal cell responses to envelopes independently of temporal frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stellate cell recording data and pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: The direct feedback pathway provides a new function by enhancing responses of ELL pyramidal cells to envelopes.
source: Our results provide a new function for this feedback pathway by showing that nP stellate cells enhance the responses of ELL pyramidal cells to envelopes.
evidence: This is a novel finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Previous studies suggested that the function of the direct feedback pathway was to enhance responses to salient stimuli, but experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis was lacking until recently.
source: Indeed, while previous studies have suggested that the function of this feedback pathway was to enhance responses to salient stimuli (Berman and Maler, 1999; Bratton and Bastian, 1990; Berman and Maler, 1998), experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis was lacking until recently when a clear role in synthesizing responses to motion stimuli consisting exclusively of first-order stimulus features was established (Clarke and Maler, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: A recent study showed that the direct feedback pathway enables neural responses to weak envelope stimuli.
source: A recent study has furthermore shown that the direct feedback pathway enables neural responses to weak envelope stimuli (Metzen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Previous studies suggested that the direct feedback pathway could function as a sensory searchlight, as originally proposed by Crick.
source: Interestingly, previous studies have suggested that the direct feedback pathway could function as a sensory searchlight (Berman and Maler, 1999), as originally proposed by Crick (Crick, 1984), thereby enhancing salient stimulus features and attenuating others.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and theoretical work.

claim: Concerted action from both direct and indirect sources of descending input is necessary for the sensory searchlight function.
source: Our results are consistent with descending input onto ELL pyramidal cells acting in this manner but instead suggest that concerted action from both direct and indirect sources is necessary.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current results in the context of previous hypotheses.

claim: The tuning function of ELL pyramidal cells must be matched to natural statistics in order to optimize coding, which ensures that behavioral sensitivity is greatest for frequencies at which natural stimuli contain the most power.
source: Overall, our results are consistent with previous ones showing that the tuning function of ELL pyramidal cells must be matched to natural statistics in order to optimize coding, which in turn ensures that behavioral sensitivity is greatest for frequencies at which natural stimuli contain the most power (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: Feedback inactivation altered ELL pyramidal cell tuning, thereby rendering coding sub-optimal, which caused a mismatch between behavioral sensitivity and natural statistics.
source: However, we found that feedback inactivation altered ELL pyramidal cell tuning, thereby rendering coding sub-optimal, which caused a mismatch between behavioral sensitivity and natural statistics.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing changes in tuning and white index after feedback inactivation.

claim: The relationship between ELL pyramidal cell and behavioral responses to envelopes is more complicated than previously expected.
source: However, our results suggest that the relationship between ELL pyramidal cell and behavioral responses to envelopes is more complicated than previously expected.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that similar changes in neural tuning led to opposite changes in behavioral tuning.

claim: It is not only the tuning exponent of ELL pyramidal cells that determines the behavioral exponent, but also the overall sensitivity.
source: Thus, it is not only the tuning exponent of ELL pyramidal cells that determines the behavioral exponent, but also the overall sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that pharmacological inactivation of both direct and indirect feedback led to similar changes in neural tuning exponent but opposite changes in behavioral tuning exponent.

claim: Previous results have demonstrated important functions for the indirect feedback pathway such as gain control.
source: Previous results have demonstrated important functions for the indirect feedback pathway such as gain control (Bastian, 1986a; Bastian, 1986b) as well as cancelation of both self and externally-generated low (<15 Hz) frequency spatially diffuse AM (i.e., first-order) stimuli (Bastian et al., 2004; Bastian, 1999; Chacron, 2006; Chacron et al., 2005; Clarke and Maler, 2017; Bastian, 1986b; Bastian, 1996a; Bastian, 1996b; Bastian, 1998), thereby allowing better detection of spatially localized stimuli (e.g., those caused by prey) (Bastian et al., 2004; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The indirect feedback pathway generates a negative image of the stimulus, thereby strongly reducing ELL pyramidal cell responses.
source: Specifically, previous studies have shown that this pathway generates a negative image of the stimulus, thereby strongly reducing ELL pyramidal cell responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous studies on the indirect feedback pathway.

claim: Short-term burst-timing dependent depression helps in sculpting the negative image generated by indirect feedback in an adaptive fashion.
source: More recent studies have shed light on how short-term burst-timing dependent depression helps in sculpting this negative image in an adaptive fashion (Bol et al., 2011; Bol et al., 2013; Mejias et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on plasticity mechanisms.

claim: The indirect feedback pathway mediates an important new function in optimized coding of envelope (i.e., second-order) stimuli by selectively attenuating responses to low frequencies.
source: In contrast, our results have demonstrated an important new function for indirect feedback in mediating optimized coding of envelope (i.e., second-order) stimuli by selectively attenuating responses to low frequencies.
evidence: This is a novel finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: SK1 channels strongly determine envelope but not AM tuning properties.
source: Previous results have shown that SK1 channels strongly determine envelope but not AM tuning properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous studies on ion channel contributions to tuning.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of SK1 channels gave rise to minimal effects on responses to AMs.
source: Specifically, pharmacological inactivation of SK1 channels gave rise to minimal effects on responses to AMs (Toporikova and Chacron, 2009) but compromised optimized coding of envelopes by causing the tuning curve to become broadband (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of SK1 channels compromised optimized coding of envelopes by causing the tuning curve to become broadband.
source: Specifically, pharmacological inactivation of SK1 channels gave rise to minimal effects on responses to AMs (Toporikova and Chacron, 2009) but compromised optimized coding of envelopes by causing the tuning curve to become broadband (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The effects of indirect feedback inactivation and of SK1 channel antagonists on ELL pyramidal cell tuning to envelopes were strikingly similar.
source: In fact, the effects of indirect feedback inactivation and of SK1 channel antagonists on ELL pyramidal cell tuning to envelopes were strikingly similar (compare our Figure 4B to Figure 6B of (Huang et al., 2016)).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data from the current study with a previous study.

claim: Indirect feedback excitation provides the necessary intracellular calcium entry that activates SK1 channels.
source: We propose that indirect feedback excitation provides the necessary intracellular calcium entry that activates SK1 channels.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: SK1 channels give rise to spike frequency adaptation, thereby selectively attenuating responses to low envelope frequencies and causing the envelope tuning curve to become high-pass.
source: These in turn give rise to spike frequency adaptation, thereby selectively attenuating responses to low envelope frequencies and causing the envelope tuning curve to become high-pass (Huang et al., 2016; Benda and Herz, 2003; Deemyad et al., 2012) (see (Huang and Chacron, 2017) for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on spike frequency adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Blocking indirect feedback input would strongly attenuate calcium entry via NMDA receptors, thereby effectively inhibiting SK1 channels.
source: Thus, blocking indirect feedback input would strongly attenuate calcium entry via NMDA receptors, thereby effectively inhibiting SK1 channels and explaining why the effects on ELL pyramidal cell tuning to envelopes are similar to those previously observed after application of SK channel antagonists (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: Calcium-permeable NMDA receptors are highly expressed within the apical dendrites of ELL pyramidal cells.
source: The fact that calcium-permeable NMDA receptors are highly expressed within the apical dendrites of ELL pyramidal cells (Harvey-Girard and Dunn, 2003; Bottai et al., 1997), where indirect feedback input terminates (Berman and Maler, 1999) and SK1 channels are located (Ellis et al., 2008), supports our hypothesis.
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Indirect feedback input terminates on the apical dendrites of ELL pyramidal cells where SK1 channels are located.
source: The fact that calcium-permeable NMDA receptors are highly expressed within the apical dendrites of ELL pyramidal cells (Harvey-Girard and Dunn, 2003; Bottai et al., 1997), where indirect feedback input terminates (Berman and Maler, 1999) and SK1 channels are located (Ellis et al., 2008), supports our hypothesis.
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The exact mechanisms by which SK1 channels determine responses to envelopes but not AMs are not well-understood.
source: However, the exact mechanisms by which SK1 channels determine responses to envelopes but not AMs, though critical in order to enable the indirect pathway to perform multiple functions, are not well-understood and should be the focus of future studies.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in understanding that requires future investigation.

claim: Multiple cell types within nP project to EGp.
source: We also note that anatomical studies have shown that multiple cell types within nP project to EGp (Sas and Maler, 1983; Sas and Maler, 1987).
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: With the exception of multipolar cells, the electrophysiological properties of nP neurons projecting to EGp are unknown.
source: However, with the exception of multipolar cells, the electrophysiological properties of these neurons are unknown to this day.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge about the electrophysiology of nP neurons.

claim: Projections from multiple nP cell types likely underlie the different functions of the indirect feedback pathway.
source: It is very likely that projections from these multiple types underlie the different functions of the indirect feedback pathway but further studies are needed to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that requires future testing.

claim: The envelope stimuli considered in the study are behaviorally relevant and contain important information as to the relative position between both conspecifics.
source: It is important to note that the envelope stimuli considered here are behaviorally relevant and contain important information as to the relative position between both conspecifics.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the behavioral significance of envelope stimuli.

claim: The indirect feedback did not attenuate responses to envelopes with higher (>0.2 Hz) frequencies.
source: Since our results show that the indirect feedback did not attenuate responses to envelopes with higher (>0.2 Hz) frequencies, it is conceivable that these could interfere with the detection of other behaviorally-relevant low frequency AM stimuli (e.g., those caused by prey) since the responses to both stimuli should be enhanced by the direct feedback pathway.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: AM stimuli caused by prey are spatially localized whereas envelope stimuli are spatially diffuse.
source: This is unlikely to be the case however because: 1) the AM stimuli caused by prey are spatially localized whereas envelope stimuli are spatially diffuse and; 2) the temporal frequency content of envelopes tends to be much lower (0 – 1 Hz) than that of prey stimuli (0 – 10 Hz) (Stamper et al., 2013; Nelson and Maciver, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing stimulus properties.

claim: The temporal frequency content of envelopes tends to be much lower (0 – 1 Hz) than that of prey stimuli (0 – 10 Hz).
source: This is unlikely to be the case however because: 1) the AM stimuli caused by prey are spatially localized whereas envelope stimuli are spatially diffuse and; 2) the temporal frequency content of envelopes tends to be much lower (0 – 1 Hz) than that of prey stimuli (0 – 10 Hz) (Stamper et al., 2013; Nelson and Maciver, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing stimulus properties.

claim: Differences in spatial extent and temporal frequency content are used by the animal to distinguish between envelope and prey stimuli.
source: We hypothesize that these differences in spatial extent and temporal frequency content are used by the animal to distinguish between both stimuli, but further studies are needed to verify that this is the case.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that requires future testing.

claim: ELL pyramidal cells displayed broadband tuning curves after pharmacological inactivation of indirect descending input.
source: The fact that ELL pyramidal cells displayed broadband tuning curves after pharmacological inactivation of indirect descending input suggests that they perform little filtering of input from stellate cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing broadband tuning after indirect feedback inactivation.

claim: ELL pyramidal cells perform little filtering of input from stellate cells.
source: The fact that ELL pyramidal cells displayed broadband tuning curves after pharmacological inactivation of indirect descending input suggests that they perform little filtering of input from stellate cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ELL pyramidal cells show broadband tuning similar to stellate cells when indirect feedback is blocked.

claim: Multipolar cells have tuning properties that are similar to those of ELL pyramidal cells and optimize coding via temporal whitening.
source: Interestingly, multipolar cells projecting indirectly have tuning properties that are similar to those of ELL pyramidal cells and optimize coding via temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning curve and white index data for multipolar cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: The output of nP received by EGp granule cells that project back to ELL is temporally whitened.
source: This result has important implications for understanding how temporal whitening of envelopes occurs in ELL pyramidal cells as it implies that the output of the nP received by EGp granule cells that project back to ELL is temporally whitened.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that multipolar cells show temporal whitening.

claim: The output of nP multipolar cells undergoes significant filtering both by EGp granule cells to enable filtering by SK1 channels in ELL pyramidal cells.
source: It is very likely that the output of nP multipolar cells, which is critical in determining ELL pyramidal cell tuning and responses to envelopes, undergoes significant filtering both by EGp granule cells to enable filtering by SK1 channels in ELL pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors about signal processing in the indirect feedback pathway.

claim: The architecture of the indirect feedback pathway shares many similarities with the cerebellum and other cerebellum-like structures.
source: It should be noted that the architecture of the indirect feedback pathway by which parallel fibers emanating from the EGp terminate onto distal ELL pyramidal cell apical dendrites shares many similarities with the cerebellum and other cerebellum-like structures (e.g., the dorsal cochlear nucleus).
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation based on established knowledge.

claim: Studies performed in cerebellum and cerebellum-like structures have shown clear common functions and mechanisms mediating how descending input attenuates or cancels responses to self-generated sensory input.
source: Studies performed in cerebellum as well as cerebellum-like structures have shown clear common functions and mechanisms mediating how such descending input in attenuating or even cancelling responses to self-generated sensory input (Cullen, 2011; Bell et al., 2008; Requarth and Sawtell, 2011; Warren and Sawtell, 2016; Sawtell, 2017; Singla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in cerebellum and cerebellum-like structures.

claim: Results showing that feedback input from parallel fibers in the cerebellar-like ELL mediate optimized coding of natural stimuli through whitening will be applicable to the cerebellum and other cerebellum-like structures.
source: It is likely that our results showing that feedback input from parallel fibers in the cerebellar-like ELL mediate optimized coding of natural stimuli through whitening will be applicable to the cerebellum as well as other cerebellum-like structures.
evidence: This is a prediction about the generalizability of the findings based on structural similarities.

claim: Descending pathways are found ubiquitously in sensory systems.
source: Finally, recent results have emphasized the critical role of descending pathways, which are found ubiquitously in sensory systems (Cajal, 1909; Holländer, 1970; Ostapoff et al., 1990; Sherman and Guillery, 2002), in determining accurate sensory neural and behavioral responses to sensory input (Manita et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies across sensory systems.

claim: Feedback terminating on the apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons was essential in determining both responses and perception to somatosensory input.
source: In particular, it was shown that feedback terminating on the apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons was essential in determining both responses and perception to somatosensory input (Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in the somatosensory system.

claim: The electrosensory system of weakly electric fish displays many documented similarities with the mammalian visual, auditory, and vestibular systems.
source: Critically, the electrosensory system of weakly electric fish displays many documented similarities with the mammalian visual, auditory, and vestibular systems (Clarke et al., 2015; Chacron et al., 2011; Metzen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Temporal whitening has been observed across sensory systems.
source: Thus, given that temporal whitening has been observed across sensory systems (Dan et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2003; Pozzorini et al., 2013; Lundstrom et al., 2010), it is likely that our results showing how feedback pathways mediate temporal whitening of sensory input by ELL pyramidal cells in the electrosensory system of weakly electric fish will be generally applicable to other systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies across different sensory systems.

claim: Results showing how feedback pathways mediate temporal whitening of sensory input by ELL pyramidal cells will be generally applicable to other systems.
source: Thus, given that temporal whitening has been observed across sensory systems (Dan et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2003; Pozzorini et al., 2013; Lundstrom et al., 2010), it is likely that our results showing how feedback pathways mediate temporal whitening of sensory input by ELL pyramidal cells in the electrosensory system of weakly electric fish will be generally applicable to other systems.
evidence: This is a prediction about the generalizability of the findings based on cross-system comparisons.

claim: The wave-type weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus was used exclusively in the present study.
source: The wave-type weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus was used exclusively in the present study.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Data obtained from ON- and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons were pooled because there is no overall difference between their responses to envelopes.
source: Data obtained from ON- and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons were pooled because, consistent with previous studies (Huang and Chacron, 2016), we found no overall difference between their responses to envelopes.
evidence: This methodological decision is justified by the current findings and consistency with previous studies.

claim: The stimuli consisted of sinusoidal AMs with constant amplitude as well as noisy EOD AMs whose envelope varied sinusoidally at different frequencies.
source: Our stimuli consisted of sinusoidal AMs with constant amplitude as well as noisy EOD AMs whose envelope varied sinusoidally at different frequencies.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli used in the study.

claim: The animal's EOD is a carrier and the meaningful stimulus is the EOD AM.
source: It is further important to realize that the animal's EOD is a carrier and that the meaningful stimulus here is the EOD AM.
evidence: This is an explanation of how to interpret the stimulus structure in the context of the animal's sensory system.

claim: Both first- and second-order features of the stimulus correspond to the second- and third-order features of the full signal received by the animal, respectively.
source: Thus, both first- and second-order features of the stimulus correspond to the second- and third-order features of the full signal received by the animal, respectively.
evidence: This is an explanation of the relationship between stimulus features and the signal received by the animal.

claim: Peripheral receptors make synaptic contact onto ELL pyramidal cells either directly with excitation for ON-type cells or indirectly via local inhibitory interneurons for OFF-type cells.
source: Peripheral receptors make synaptic contact onto ELL pyramidal cells either directly with excitation for ON-type cells or indirectly via local inhibitory interneurons for OFF-type cells.
evidence: This is established anatomical and physiological knowledge about the electrosensory system.

claim: Pyramidal cells are the sole output neurons of the ELL and project to the midbrain torus semicircularis (TS) which in turn projects to higher brain areas.
source: Pyramidal cells are the sole output neurons of the ELL and project to the midbrain torus semicircularis (TS) which in turn projects to higher brain areas.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the electrosensory system.

claim: Injecting lidocaine into PET will block indirect feedback input to most if not all pyramidal cells within the ipsilateral ELL.
source: We note that injecting lidocaine into PET will block indirect feedback input to most if not all pyramidal cells within the ipsilateral ELL.
evidence: This is an explanation of the expected effect of the pharmacological manipulation based on anatomy.

claim: Injecting CNQX into the ELL molecular layer will only block indirect feedback input in the vicinity of the ELL being recorded from.
source: In contrast, injecting CNQX into the ELL molecular layer will only block indirect feedback input in the vicinity of the ELL being recorded from (Chacron et al., 2005; Bastian, 1993).
evidence: This is an explanation of the expected effect of the pharmacological manipulation based on previous studies.

claim: Movement envelopes are fundamentally different than 'social' envelopes that are due to interaction between the EODs of three or more fish.
source: We note that movement envelopes, which are the focus of the current study, are fundamentally different than so-called 'social' envelopes that are instead due to interaction between the EODs of three of more fish (Stamper et al., 2013) and which have been the focus of previous studies (Middleton et al., 2006; Stamper et al., 2012; Savard et al., 2011; McGillivray et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This distinction is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing different types of envelope stimuli.

claim: For social envelopes, the frequency content of the envelope is mostly determined by the frequencies of the three EODs.
source: Indeed, for social envelopes, the frequency content of the envelope is mostly determined by the frequencies of the three EODs.
evidence: This is an explanation of the physical basis of social envelope generation.

claim: For movement envelopes occurring during interactions between two conspecifics, the envelope frequency content is determined solely by the relative movements of both fish.
source: In contrast, for movement envelopes occurring during interactions between two conspecifics, the envelope frequency content is not determined by the two EOD frequencies or the resulting beat frequency. Rather, it is determined solely by the relative movements of both fish (Fotowat et al., 2013; Metzen and Chacron, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing movement envelopes.

claim: Field studies have shown that Apteronotid species tend to encounter movement envelopes much more frequently than social envelopes.
source: We further note that field studies have shown that Apteronotid species tend to encounter movement envelopes much more frequently than social envelopes: this is because they tend to be found in groups of 2 much more frequently than in groups of 3+ (Stamper et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a field study.

claim: Social envelopes are expected to be more relevant for weakly electric fish species that tend to be more gregarious (e.g., Eigenmannia virescens).
source: It is expected that social envelopes will be more relevant for weakly electric fish species that tend to be more gregarious (e.g., Eigenmannia virescens).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the social behavior of different species.

claim: Stellate cells have low spontaneous firing rates (1.37 ± 0.42 Hz) and do not respond to high AM frequencies.
source: While stellate cells have low spontaneous firing rates (1.37 ± 0.42 Hz) and do not respond to high AM frequencies, multipolar cells have high spontaneous firing rates (55.53 ± 8.05 Hz and do respond well to high AM frequencies > 32 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from the current study.

claim: Multipolar cells have high spontaneous firing rates (55.53 ± 8.05 Hz) and respond well to high AM frequencies > 32 Hz.
source: While stellate cells have low spontaneous firing rates (1.37 ± 0.42 Hz) and do not respond to high AM frequencies, multipolar cells have high spontaneous firing rates (55.53 ± 8.05 Hz and do respond well to high AM frequencies > 32 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from the current study.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of stellate and multipolar cells match the results found in the literature.
source: These results match the results found in the literature (Bastian and Bratton, 1990; Bratton and Bastian, 1990), confirming our recordings were appropriate.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies and validates the current recordings.

claim: Multipolar cells have significantly higher baseline firing rates than stellate cells.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Bastian and Bratton, 1990; Bratton and Bastian, 1990), multipolar cells have significantly higher baseline firing rates than stellate cells (χ2 = 12, p=5.32*10- 4, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of baseline firing rates shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation significantly decreased the power law exponent of ELL pyramidal cell tuning curves.
source: Population-averaged best-fit power law exponents before (black) and after (purple) lidocaine injection were significantly different from one another (p=0.0156, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4B inset.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation significantly decreased the white index of ELL pyramidal cell responses.
source: Population-averaged white index values before (black) and after (purple) lidocaine application were significantly different from one another (p=0.0234, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4F left panel.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation significantly decreased neural sensitivity to envelopes.
source: Population-averaged relative changes in neural (left) and behavioral (right) gain following lidocaine application were both significantly different from zero (neuron: p=4.77*10−4, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test, behavior: p=0.002, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4F right panel.

claim: Complete feedback inactivation significantly decreased behavioral sensitivity to envelopes.
source: Population-averaged relative changes in neural (left) and behavioral (right) gain following lidocaine application were both significantly different from zero (neuron: p=4.77*10−4, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test, behavior: p=0.002, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4F right panel.

claim: Indirect feedback inactivation significantly decreased the power law exponent of ELL pyramidal cell tuning curves.
source: Population-averaged best-fit power law exponent before (black) and after (orange) lidocaine injection (p=0.0039, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5B inset.

claim: Indirect feedback inactivation significantly decreased the white index of ELL pyramidal cell responses.
source: Population-averaged white index before (black) and after (orange) lidocaine application (p=0.0273, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5F left panel.

claim: Indirect feedback inactivation significantly increased neural sensitivity to envelopes.
source: Population-averaged relative changes in neural and behavioral sensitivity following lidocaine application (neuron: p=7.03*10−6, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test, behavior: p=6.74*10−4, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5F right panel.

claim: Indirect feedback inactivation significantly increased behavioral sensitivity to envelopes.

evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5F right panel.

claim: The power law exponents of stellate and multipolar cells were significantly different from one another.
source: In both cases, values obtained for stellate and multipolar cells were significantly different from one another (exponent: χ2 = 12, p=5.32*10 - 4, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; white index: χ2 = 10.7, p=0.0011, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6E.

source: In both cases, values obtained for stellate and multipolar cells were significantly different from one another (exponent: χ2 = 12, p=5.32*10 - 4, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; white index: χ2 = 10.7, p=0.0011, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA).
